messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 70

He is thirty-six now, a tax consultant with a tidy home office and a calendar blocked in careful color-coded increments, the kind of man clients trust with deadlines and numbers because he rarely misses either. He is married, and from the outside his life looks measured and stable. But when he tells his story, it always begins with the deployment he took in his twenties, when structure and discipline still felt simple, before danger began attaching itself to ordinary things.

He serves in the military for several years and spends most of that time believing he can handle what comes. The event he returns to most often happens during a convoy overseas. He remembers the heat first, and the boredom that had settled over the morning, everyone alert but dulled by routine. Then the explosion. He does not tell it dramatically. He says there is a flash, a sound he feels more than hears, and then the world becomes dirt, smoke, shouting, and the metallic taste of fear. He sees one of the men he knows badly injured. He remembers trying to move, trying to respond the way he was trained, while another part of him is stunned by how quickly an ordinary morning becomes irreversible. Later, what stays with him is not only the horror of the attack, but the helplessness of surviving it. He comes home carrying the conviction that he should have done something more, something different, though he cannot say exactly what.

At first, after returning home, he expects the unease to pass. Instead, it follows him into civilian life. Loud noises make his body jerk before his mind catches up. Fireworks on summer holidays send him scanning for exits. The pop of a tire on the highway leaves his hands shaking on the steering wheel. He does not like having his back to doors. In restaurants he chooses the seat facing the room, then insists it is just a habit. At night he sleeps lightly, waking abruptly, heart pounding, disoriented for a few seconds before he recognizes his bedroom. Some nights he dreams of the convoy in fragments—the blast, the dust, the feeling that someone needs him and he cannot get there in time. He wakes already tense, as if he has been bracing for impact in his sleep.

His wife notices the changes before he is ready to name them. Early in their marriage, she reaches for him unexpectedly from behind while he is washing dishes, and he spins around so fast that they both freeze. He apologizes over and over, ashamed by the look on her face. He becomes irritable in ways that do not fit the life he has built. Small inconveniences—a slow driver, a barking dog, a cluttered countertop—provoke bursts of anger that flare and leave him embarrassed. He says he feels “on” all the time, as if something inside him is continuously scanning for threat. Relaxation feels unsafe, almost irresponsible.

His work suits some parts of him. As a tax consultant, he can disappear into precision: spreadsheets, schedules, reconciliations, clean columns of numbers that balance when the world inside him does not. During tax season he works long hours and tells himself busyness is just professionalism. In quieter moments, though, concentration slips. A client’s question will drift past him because he is suddenly back in the convoy, replaying details he does not want and cannot stop. If someone drops a file or slams a door down the hall, his body reacts before he can hide it. He has become known as dependable but intense. Coworkers joke that he is “serious about everything.” They do not see how much effort goes into appearing composed.

Over the years his world narrows. He avoids news about war. He skips crowded events, then invents practical reasons not to go. He no longer attends neighborhood Fourth of July gatherings. He sits through family celebrations with his jaw tight, tracking every noise. He drinks more than he means to on some evenings, not to get drunk exactly, but to dull the edge enough to sleep. Even then, rest does not come easily. He says he is tired all the time, but never at peace.

What troubles him most is not just fear, but distance. He loves his wife and feels guilty that she often gets a guarded version of him. She tells him he seems far away even when he is sitting beside her on the couch. He knows what she means. There are moments when he looks at his life—the marriage, the steady work, the safety of home—and feels detached from it, as though he is watching someone else inhabit the future he was supposed to be grateful for. He wants to be present, to be softer, to believe the danger is over. Instead he moves through each day braced, exhausted by vigilance, carrying a war that does not stay in the past.
